title: Smart Vault Security in Banks: A Quantum AI-Enabled Intrusion Detection System
journal_or_venue: 2025 International Conference on Engineering Innovations and Technologies (ICoEIT)
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical intrusion detection system (QAID) for bank smart vault security that uses quantum feature encoding and quantum kernel methods with a QSVM classifier to detect complex, high-dimensional intrusion patterns. Experiments on a real-world smart vault dataset and synthetic data show improved detection accuracy, robustness to high-dimensional data, and near real-time capability; future work targets deployment on near-term quantum hardware and scaling to additional data modalities.
methodology_description: The authors propose and implement a hybrid quantum-classical intrusion detection pipeline (QAID/QAI-ID) for smart vault security. Multimodal security data (access logs, biometric scores, IoT sensor readings, network indicators) are preprocessed (missing values mean-imputed, features normalized to [0,1], optional feature selection/extraction) and mapped into quantum states via a parameterized unitary U(x) implemented with rotation gates (quantum feature encoding; amplitude/feature-map style encodings are described). Pairwise similarities between encoded states are computed as a quantum kernel K(x_i,x_j) := |<phi(x_i)|phi(x_j)>|^2 using statevector simulation, producing a kernel matrix used to train a Support Vector Machine (classical SVM with a custom quantum kernel / QSVM paradigm). The SVM quadratic program is solved for Lagrange multipliers and bias; classification of new samples follows the standard kernel SVM decision function sign(sum_i alpha_i y_i K(x_i,x_new) + b). The system is integrated for real-time operation via an API receiving IoT/biometric/access-log streams; detected anomalies trigger alerts/response modules. Experiments include both a proprietary real-world smart-vault security dataset and a synthetic dataset (1,000 samples × 50 features) for controlled evaluation. Evaluation metrics reported include accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC and per-sample classification latency. Quantum elements were simulated with Qiskit and PennyLane (statevector simulator) and classical components implemented in Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn). Regularization parameter C for the SVM was optimized by cross-validation.

results_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid Quantum AI Intrusion Detection system (QAID) for smart vault security that encodes classical security features into quantum feature maps and builds a QSVM via a quantum kernel. In simulation and experiments on a synthetic dataset and a reported real-world smart-vault dataset, the authors report high detection performance (F1 up to 97.5%, ROC-AUC 0.98) and low per-sample classification latency (0.015s on an Intel i9). They further report improvements versus a classical SVM baseline (~4–6% absolute gains on key metrics) and show resilience under simulated adversarial attacks. The authors argue these results indicate potential benefits of quantum-kernel methods for high-dimensional intrusion detection, while noting deployment on actual quantum hardware and further scalability remain future work.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — QSVM with a quantum kernel (state-overlap kernel computed via statevector simulation) achieves reported gains of ~4–6% over a classical SVM baseline on both synthetic and proprietary real-world smart-vault datasets (e.g., F1 97.5% synthetic, accuracy ~96.5% real-world).

#idea:hybrid-approach — Hybrid pipeline: classical preprocessing and SVM training using a precomputed quantum kernel (quantum feature encoding + classical SVM quadratic solver) enables integration into near-real-time operational workflows.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Authors argue near-term deployment potential and real-time capability (mean classification time reported ~0.015s in synthetic tests), and suggest future porting to NISQ hardware.
#limitation:simulation-only — All quantum kernel computations were performed via statevector simulation (Qiskit/PennyLane); no experiments on actual quantum hardware were reported.
#limitation:qubit-count — The paper does not specify qubit counts, circuit depth, or resource estimates for porting the feature map to real QPUs, limiting assessment of practical feasibility.
#limitation:noise — The evaluation ignores noise and sampling error (statevector backend, no shot-based runs or noise modelling), so robustness on real noisy devices is untested.

#limitation:data-encoding — While rotation-based and amplitude encodings are described, the computational cost and scalability of encoding high-dimensional multimodal bank data into quantum states is not quantified.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Real-world dataset is proprietary and dataset size is unspecified; quantum components are not validated on hardware, reducing reproducibility and external validation.
contradictions: contradiction:scalability — The paper claims near-term deployment and real-time capability on bank systems but provides no qubit counts, circuit-depth, noise modelling, or hardware experiments; scaling from statevector simulation to real QPUs remains unsubstantiated.

contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — A reported 4–6% improvement over a classical SVM baseline is presented as a quantum advantage, yet the experiment uses a quantum-inspired kernel computed in simulation without isolating whether gains stem from the feature map choice, kernel design, or quantum-specific effects; no ablation isolates the quantum contribution.
